title: How would you design a real-time COLLABORATIVE DOCUMENT editor like Google Docs — the core problem is merging CONCURRENT edits from many users without conflicts, so you need either Operational Transformation (OT: transform each incoming op against concurrent ops so all replicas converge, typically via a central server that orders operations) or CRDTs (Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: structures that merge commutatively so replicas converge WITHOUT a central coordinator) — plus persisting the op log / document snapshots, WebSockets for low-latency bidirectional sync, presence/cursors, offline edit buffering + replay on reconnect, and the trade-off between OT (simpler data, needs a server to order ops) and CRDTs (coordination-free, better for offline/P2P, but larger metadata)?
shortTitle: How would you design a real-time collaborative document editor like Google Docs (OT vs CRDT)

s1_definition.profdef: A collaborative editor lets many users edit the same document simultaneously and guarantees all their replicas converge to the same final state despite concurrent edits. The two merge strategies are Operational Transformation, where each operation is transformed against concurrent operations so that applying them in different orders yields the same result, usually coordinated by a central server that assigns a total order, and Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, where the document is a data structure whose merge is commutative and associative so replicas converge without any central coordinator. Both are paired with a persisted operation log and periodic snapshots, low-latency bidirectional sync over WebSockets, presence and cursor sharing, and offline edit buffering with replay on reconnect.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh and Priya at National Bank of India both editing the same loan agreement at the same time. Rajesh inserts a word at the start while Priya deletes a word in the middle, in the same instant. If we naively apply both, their positions no longer line up and the document becomes garbled. Operational Transformation is like a careful clerk who, when Priya's edit arrives after Rajesh's, adjusts Priya's "delete position 10" to "delete position 11" because Rajesh's insert shifted everything right, so both edits land correctly. CRDTs are a cleverer paper design where every character has a permanent unique ID instead of a position, so insertions and deletions never clash no matter the order, and no central clerk is needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: The hard problem is merging concurrent edits so all replicas converge; OT transforms ops against each other with a central ordering server, while CRDTs use commutative structures that merge coordination-free, both backed by an op log, WebSocket sync, and offline replay.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A collaborative editor lets many users edit the same document simultaneously and guarantees all their replicas converge to the same final state despite concurrent edits. The two merge strategies are Operational Transformation, where each operation is transformed against concurrent operations so that applying them in different orders yields the same result, usually coordinated by a central server that assigns a total order, and Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, where the document is a data structure whose merge is commutative and associative so replicas converge without any central coordinator. Both are paired with a persisted operation log and periodic snapshots, low-latency bidirectional sync over WebSockets, presence and cursor sharing, and offline edit buffering with replay on reconnect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh and Priya at National Bank of India both editing the same loan agreement at the same time. Rajesh inserts a word at the start while Priya deletes a word in the middle, in the same instant. If we naively apply both, their positions no longer line up and the document becomes garbled. Operational Transformation is like a careful clerk who, when Priya's edit arrives after Rajesh's, adjusts Priya's "delete position 10" to "delete position 11" because Rajesh's insert shifted everything right, so both edits land correctly. CRDTs are a cleverer paper design where every character has a permanent unique ID instead of a position, so insertions and deletions never clash no matter the order, and no central clerk is needed.

**One line to remember:** The hard problem is merging concurrent edits so all replicas converge; OT transforms ops against each other with a central ordering server, while CRDTs use commutative structures that merge coordination-free, both backed by an op log, WebSocket sync, and offline replay.

sections.s2_technical:
The core problem. Multiple users edit the same text concurrently. Each edit is an operation like "insert 'x' at position 5" or "delete the character at position 10". The trouble is that positions are relative to the document state, and when two edits happen concurrently on different replicas, applying them in different orders gives different results, so replicas diverge. You need a scheme where concurrent operations merge to the same final document everywhere, which is called convergence or strong eventual consistency.

Operational Transformation. OT keeps operations position-based but transforms them. When operation B arrives having been generated concurrently with operation A that was already applied, the server transforms B against A so B's positions account for A's effect. For example, if A inserted a character before B's target position, B's position is shifted by one. The transformation function is defined so that applying A then transformed-B gives the same result as applying B then transformed-A. OT typically relies on a central server to assign a total order to operations and to perform transformations, which keeps the client data simple (plain text plus integer positions) but means the server is a required coordinator and the transformation logic is famously tricky to get exactly right, especially for rich text.

CRDTs. A CRDT replaces fragile positions with stable identities. In a sequence CRDT each inserted character gets a globally unique, ordered identifier (for example a fractional position or a dense ordered ID plus a site ID), and the document is the set of these identified characters sorted by their IDs. Insertions place a new ID between two existing IDs, and deletions mark an ID as removed (a tombstone). Because every operation commutes, applying them in any order on any replica yields the same set and therefore the same document, with no transformation and no central coordinator needed. This makes CRDTs ideal for offline and peer-to-peer editing. The cost is metadata: every character carries an ID, and tombstones linger, so the structure is larger and needs garbage collection.

The trade-off. OT has simpler, smaller data and is well-understood for server-coordinated editing, which is why classic Google Docs used OT, but it needs a central server to order and transform operations and the transform functions are hard to prove correct. CRDTs need no central coordinator and handle offline and P2P gracefully, but carry heavier per-character metadata and tombstone overhead. Modern systems often choose CRDTs (like Yjs or Automerge) for their robustness and offline-first behavior, accepting the metadata cost, while server-centric products may still use OT.

Persistence: op log plus snapshots. You never keep the document only in memory. You persist the ordered log of operations, which is the authoritative history and lets any replica rebuild the document by replaying ops. Replaying millions of ops is slow, so you periodically write a snapshot of the materialized document and keep only the ops since the last snapshot, so recovery is "load latest snapshot, replay the tail". The op log also powers undo, audit, and version history.

WebSockets for sync. Editing needs instant bidirectional updates, so each client holds a WebSocket to the server (or peers). Local edits are applied optimistically on the client immediately for a snappy feel, sent over the socket, merged via OT or CRDT, and the merged result broadcast to all other clients, which apply it. Because the merge converges, every client ends at the same document.

Presence and cursors. Users want to see who else is editing and where their cursors and selections are. These are ephemeral signals broadcast over the same socket, not part of the durable op log, and they update in real time and expire when a user leaves. With CRDTs, cursor positions are often expressed as references to character IDs so they stay correct even as text shifts.

Offline buffering and replay. A user may lose connection and keep editing. The client buffers its local operations while offline. On reconnect it replays them to the server (OT transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile; CRDT simply merges them since ops commute), and pulls the operations it missed. CRDTs shine here because offline edits merge without a central transform step. The result is that offline work is never lost and merges cleanly.

The senior nuance is convergence plus intention preservation. Convergence means all replicas end identical; intention preservation means each user's edit still means what they intended after merging. OT and CRDTs both aim for convergence; preserving intention for complex concurrent edits (like formatting overlaps) is the genuinely hard part, and it is why rich-text collaboration is much harder than plain text.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India lets a customer and a relationship manager co-edit a loan agreement in real time. Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) both edit the same document.

Problem 1 — concurrent edits garbled the document. Rajesh inserted text at the start while Priya deleted text in the middle at the same instant; naive application left both edits pointing at wrong positions and corrupted the agreement. This is why we need OT to transform concurrent operations, or a CRDT whose operations commute.

Problem 2 — a crash lost recent edits because the document lived only in memory. This is why we persist an ordered op log plus periodic snapshots, so the document rebuilds exactly.

Problem 3 — Priya edited on a train with no signal and feared losing her work. This is why we buffer offline edits on the client and replay-merge them on reconnect.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of both strategies on a shared text document: an OT engine that transforms an incoming insert/delete against a concurrent one, a simple sequence-CRDT that assigns ordered character IDs so edits commute, an op log with snapshotting, and an offline buffer that replays on reconnect. It runs Rajesh's and Priya's concurrent edits through both engines and shows both converge to the same text.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: base document "Loan amount Rs". Rajesh inserts "Home " at position 0; Priya inserts " 500000" at position 14. These are concurrent.

Step 1 (OT path): The server orders the operations, applying Rajesh's insert first, giving "Home Loan amount Rs". Now Priya's insert at position 14 is stale because Rajesh added 5 characters at the front, so everything shifted right by 5.

Step 2 (OT path): The engine transforms Priya's operation against Rajesh's. Because Rajesh inserted 5 characters at a position at or before Priya's target, Priya's position 14 becomes 19. Applying the transformed insert yields "Home Loan amount Rs 500000", correct and converged.

Step 3 (CRDT path): Each character already has a stable ordered ID. Rajesh inserts "Home " by creating IDs before the first character's ID; Priya inserts " 500000" by creating IDs after the last. These IDs do not depend on each other's positions.

Step 4 (CRDT path): Merging Rajesh's replica into Priya's, or Priya's into Rajesh's, is just a set union of identified characters, which is commutative. Both merge orders sort the characters by their IDs and produce exactly the same text "Home Loan amount Rs 500000", with no transformation and no central coordinator.

Step 5 (persistence): Each applied operation is appended to the op log. After every 1000 ops a snapshot of the materialized document is written and older ops truncated, so recovery loads the snapshot and replays only the tail.

Step 6 (offline): Priya edits on a train with no signal, inserting "URGENT: ". The offline buffer records it. On reconnect the buffered op is replayed and merged, OT transforming it against everything that happened meanwhile, or the CRDT simply merging since ops commute, so her offline work is never lost.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Base document: "Loan amount Rs"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] OT converged result:   "Home Loan amount Rs 500000"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] CRDT merge (R then P): "Home Loan amount Rs 500000"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] CRDT merge (P then R): "Home Loan amount Rs 500000"
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] CRDT order-independent: true
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] OpLog size=2 (replay rebuilds document; snapshot every 1000 ops)
2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ] Offline edits buffered: 1 → replayed+merged on reconnect
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The core problem in a collaborative editor is merging concurrent edits from many users so that every replica converges to the same final document, which is strong eventual consistency. Edits are operations like insert a character at a position or delete a character at a position, and the difficulty is that positions are relative to the document state, so when two edits happen concurrently on different replicas and are applied in different orders, the replicas diverge and the document garbles. I solve this with one of two strategies: Operational Transformation or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types.

Operational Transformation keeps operations position-based but transforms them against each other. When an operation arrives that was generated concurrently with one already applied, the server transforms it so its positions account for the earlier operation's effect, for example shifting a position right by the length of a concurrent insert, and the transform is defined so applying A then transformed-B equals applying B then transformed-A. OT keeps the client data simple, just text and integer positions, which is why classic Google Docs used it, but it needs a central server to assign a total order and perform the transforms, and the transformation functions are famously hard to prove correct, especially for rich text. CRDTs take the opposite approach: every inserted character gets a stable, globally unique, ordered identity instead of a fragile position, and the document is the set of identified characters sorted by their IDs. Insertions place a new ID between two existing IDs and deletions mark a tombstone, and because every operation commutes, merging replicas in any order yields the same result with no transformation and no central coordinator, which makes CRDTs ideal for offline and peer-to-peer editing. The cost is heavier per-character metadata and lingering tombstones that need garbage collection.

That is the trade-off I state plainly: OT has simpler, smaller data but requires a central ordering server and tricky transform logic, while CRDTs are coordination-free and offline-friendly but carry more metadata, which is why modern libraries like Yjs and Automerge favor CRDTs and accept the overhead. Around whichever engine I choose, I persist an ordered operation log as the authoritative history so any replica can rebuild the document by replaying ops, and because replaying millions of ops is slow I write periodic snapshots and keep only the tail since the last snapshot, which also powers undo and version history.

For the live experience I use WebSockets so edits sync bidirectionally with low latency: the client applies its own edit optimistically for a snappy feel, sends it over the socket, the server or peers merge it via OT or CRDT, and the merged result broadcasts to everyone. Presence and cursors ride the same socket as ephemeral signals that are not in the durable op log, and with CRDTs cursors reference character IDs so they stay correct as text shifts. Offline editing is handled by buffering local operations on the client while disconnected and replaying them on reconnect, where OT transforms them against everything that happened meanwhile and a CRDT simply merges since operations commute, so work done on a train with no signal is never lost. On my project at National Bank of India, this is how a customer and a relationship manager co-edit a loan agreement in real time without the concurrent-edit corruption we originally hit.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that the hard problem is converging concurrent edits, which I solve with OT that transforms operations against each other using a central ordering server, or with CRDTs that use commutative identified structures to merge coordination-free and offline, and I back either with a persisted op log plus snapshots, WebSocket optimistic sync, ephemeral presence and cursors, and offline buffering with replay on reconnect.
